learn: What summarisation is and where it is used
The three dimensions: extractive vs abstractive, single vs multi-document, generic vs query-focused
The extractive pipeline: content selection, information ordering, sentence realisation
Abstractive summarisation with seq2seq, attention and Transformers
intro.why: Summarisation is one of the most used NLP applications (search snippets, meeting notes, news digests). It brings together earlier sessions: TF-IDF and cosine similarity (M2), graph ranking, sequence-to-sequence models with attention (M11), and evaluation by overlap with references.

symbols: term frequency in document j, inverse document frequency
similarity of sentence s to the query/topic
MMR trade-off between relevance and novelty

sections.title: The summarisation task and its uses
sections.plain: Produce a shorter text that keeps the key information.
sections.body:
An executive wakes up to 150 unread emails, a 60-page industry report and transcripts of three missed meetings: they need the TL;DR. Text summarisation produces an abridged version of a text that retains its key, relevant information. People do it naturally (retelling a 400-page novel in three minutes); for a computer, deciding what is important is hard.

Applications: search engines' short answer snippets (around 26 words for a definitional query); action items from chat logs and emails; news digests; meeting minutes; and accessibility, simplifying medical or legal text for non-experts.

sections.title: Extractive vs abstractive, single vs multi-document, generic vs query-focused
sections.plain: Decide what the summary is made of, what it reads, and what it focuses on.
sections.body:
• Output: extractive summaries copy the most important sentences verbatim (a highlighter); abstractive summaries rewrite the content in new words (a pen), possibly using vocabulary absent from the source.
  • Input: single-document (a headline or abstract for one article; for news, simply taking the first sentence, the lead baseline, is surprisingly strong) vs multi-document (one overview from five reports on an earthquake), which must handle overlapping facts, contradictions and heavy redundancy.
  • Focus: generic (what is this page about?) vs query-focused (summarise only what answers "Was cast-metal movable type invented in Korea?"), effectively a question-answering tool.

sections.title: The extractive pipeline
sections.plain: Select content, order it, then polish the sentences.
sections.body:
Extractive summarisation is historically the most reliable approach because it copies source sentences and so can't invent facts. It follows three stages:

  1. Content selection: segment into sentences and score them; keep the best (while avoiding redundancy).
  2. Information ordering: arrange the selected sentences coherently.
  3. Sentence realisation: simplify and fix the sentences so they read well out of context.

Weaknesses: choppy transitions, redundancy across documents, dangling references, and sentences that are longer than needed, which the later stages address.

sections.title: Frequency and TF-IDF content selection
sections.plain: Important words are frequent in this document but not everywhere; sentences full of them are important.
sections.body:
Luhn's idea (1958): a document about Mars repeats "Mars", "rover", "crater". Raw frequency also rewards function words, so weight words by TF-IDF:

$$\text{weight}(w_i) = TF_{ij}\times IDF_i,\qquad IDF_i = \log\frac{N}{df_i}$$

A sentence scores highly if it contains many high-weight (salient) words; averaging over its words avoids simply favouring long sentences. In the code example, "mars" (weight 7.15), "rover" and "crater" (4.6 each) dominate; Mars sentences score 3.2–3.6 and the off-topic bakery sentence 2.57, so it is never selected.

Supervised variants learn sentence scores from features (position, length, salient words, cue phrases) using document–summary pairs.

sections.title: LexRank: graph centrality
sections.plain: A sentence that many others are similar to is central, so it represents the main theme.
sections.body:
Picture sentences at a cocktail party: they "talk" when they share similar words, and the person most others agree with is the central figure. LexRank builds a graph with sentences as nodes and edges weighted by cosine similarity (often keeping only edges above a threshold), then runs a PageRank-style iteration:

$$r(u) = \frac{1-d}{N} + d\sum_{v\to u}\frac{w_{vu}}{\sum_{z}w_{vz}}\,r(v)$$

The highest-ranked sentences are extracted. Centrality rewards sentences that summarise what many others say, and an off-topic sentence (the bakery line) gets almost no centrality (0.025 vs ≈ 0.2 in the code example). TextRank is the same idea; both are unsupervised.

sections.title: MMR: relevance vs redundancy
sections.plain: Pick sentences that are relevant but not repeats of what you already chose.
sections.body:
Summarising articles about J.K. Rowling's lawsuit: S1 "Rowling won her legal battle to ban an unofficial encyclopedia" (relevance 0.90) and S2 "A US judge ruled in favour of Rowling against the encyclopedia's publication" (0.88) say nearly the same thing. Taking the top two by relevance gives a redundant summary.

$$\hat s_{MMR} = \arg\max_{s\in D\setminus S}\Big[\lambda\,\text{Sim}(s, Q) - (1-\lambda)\max_{s_j\in S}\text{Sim}(s, s_j)\Big]$$

Add the best sentence greedily until the length limit. Worked (λ = 0.5; Sim(S1, S2) = 0.85, Sim(S1, S3) = 0.35): first S1 (0.45); then S2 scores 0.44 − 0.425 = 0.015 while S3 (relevance 0.70) scores 0.35 − 0.175 = 0.175, so S3 is chosen. With λ = 1 MMR reduces to plain relevance ranking (S1, S2). MMR is a greedy approximation to choosing the best set.

sections.title: Information ordering
sections.plain: Arrange the chosen sentences so the summary reads as a story.
sections.body:
Sentences from five documents in random order "sound like a madman talking". Strategies:

  • Chronological: by the date of the source (or event), natural for news.
  • Coherence: neighbouring sentences should share entities or have high cosine similarity.
  • Topical templates (from information extraction) for specific question types:
question typeinformation flow
Biographydates → nationality → education → fame
Definitiongenus → species → synonym → subtype
Medical / drugpopulation → problem → intervention → outcome

sections.title: Sentence realisation
sections.plain: Trim sentences and fix references so they make sense on their own.
sections.body:
Simplification (pruning): remove appositives, attribution clauses and initial adverbials that cost length without adding key content. "Rebels agreed to talks with government officials, international observers said Tuesday." → "Rebels agreed to talks with government officials."

Context fixes (anaphora resolution): a sentence starting "He has immunity from prosecution…" is meaningless out of context; replace the pronoun with its referent: "Gen. Augusto Pinochet has immunity from prosecution…". Similarly, expand first mentions of names and remove discourse connectives ("However,") that refer to unextracted text.

Pruning frees space for more content within the length limit; parsing (M9–M10) identifies the removable constituents.

sections.title: Abstractive summarisation with seq2seq and Transformers
sections.plain: Read the whole document, then write a new summary word by word, looking back at relevant parts.
sections.body:
Early neural summarisers used RNNs, which forgot the beginning of long documents. Sequence-to-sequence with attention (M11) changed this: the encoder reads the document into representations; the decoder writes the summary one token at a time; attention lets each step look back at the most relevant input words.

Today's systems use Transformers (multi-head attention), either encoder–decoder models or decoder-only LLMs. For decoder-only training, examples are formatted as ARTICLE <EOS> SUMMARY <EOS> <pad>, and the loss is computed only on the summary tokens; the article is context.

Abstractive summaries are fluent and compact and can merge information across sentences, but they can hallucinate facts (e.g. "found traces of life" when the source says "will search"), so faithfulness checks matter. Long inputs strain context windows (chunk-then-summarise, or retrieval).

sections.title: ROUGE evaluation
sections.plain: Count how many of the human summaries' n-grams the system summary contains.
sections.body:
ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) compares a system summary X with human reference summaries by n-gram overlap:

$$\text{ROUGE-N} = \frac{\sum_{S\in\text{Refs}}\sum_{g\in S}\min(\text{count}(g, X), \text{count}(g, S))}{\sum_{S\in\text{Refs}}\sum_{g\in S}\text{count}(g, S)}$$

"Of all the n-word phrases the humans used, what fraction did the system include?" Worked ("What is water spinach?"): references H1 "Water spinach is a green leafy vegetable grown in the tropics" (10 bigrams), H2 "Water spinach is a semi-aquatic tropical plant grown as a vegetable" (10), H3 "Water spinach is a commonly eaten leaf vegetable of Asia" (9). System: "Water spinach is a leaf vegetable commonly eaten in tropical areas of Asia." Bigram matches 3, 3 and 6 (water spinach, spinach is, is a; plus commonly eaten, leaf vegetable, of Asia with H3), so ROUGE-2 = 12/29 ≈ 0.41. ROUGE-1 = 22/32 ≈ 0.69.

Variants: ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence), precision/F versions. Limitation: it rewards shared wording, not meaning, so valid paraphrases score low and fluent but unfaithful summaries can score well. Complement it with human judgement and faithfulness checks.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Lead-3 (first three sentences) is a strong news baseline because journalists put key facts first.
  • Embedding-based metrics (e.g. BERTScore) compare meaning rather than exact words.
  • Query-focused MDS combines retrieval (M14) with MMR-style selection.
  • Length control: compare systems only at equal summary lengths; longer summaries trivially raise recall-based ROUGE.

code.title: TF-IDF scoring, LexRank and the lead baseline
code.explain: Weights words Luhn-style (TF in this document × IDF from a wider collection: mars 7.15, rover/crater 4.6), scores sentences by average weight (Mars sentences 3.2–3.6, bakery 2.57), builds a cosine-similarity graph and runs LexRank power iteration (bakery centrality 0.025), and shows the lead-1 baseline.
mistakes: Scoring by raw frequency (stop words win).
Returning sentences in score order instead of document order.
code.notes: IDF from a tiny background set; real systems use large collections.
code.code:
"""Extractive content selection: TF-IDF sentence scores, LexRank centrality, and the lead baseline."""
import numpy as np, re
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

doc = """The rover landed safely on Mars after a seven-month journey.
Engineers cheered as the first images from the Mars surface arrived.
The rover will search the crater for signs of ancient microbial life.
Mars once had rivers and lakes, making the crater a promising site.
The mission also tests technology for future human trips to Mars.
Meanwhile, a local bakery announced a new bread recipe.""".split("\n")
background = ["Bread recipes and bakery news from the town.", "Stock markets rose on Tuesday.",
              "The football team won its match.", "Engineers build bridges and roads."]

vec = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english").fit(doc + background)   # IDF from a wider collection
X = vec.transform(doc)
# Luhn-style: weight each word by its frequency in THIS document x IDF, then score sentences
an = vec.build_analyzer(); vocab = vec.vocabulary_; idf = vec.idf_
tf = {}
for sent in doc:
    for w in an(sent): tf[w] = tf.get(w, 0) + 1
weight = {w: tf[w] * idf[vocab[w]] for w in tf}
print("top word weights:", sorted(((round(float(v), 2), w) for w, v in weight.items()), reverse=True)[:4])
tfidf_score = np.array([sum(weight[w] for w in set(an(sent))) / max(1, len(set(an(sent)))) for sent in doc])
print("TF-IDF sentence scores (mean weight of its words):")
for s_, v in sorted(zip(doc, tfidf_score), key=lambda x: -x[1]): print(f"  {v:.3f}  {s_[:60]}")

# LexRank: cosine-similarity graph + PageRank-style power iteration
S = cosine_similarity(X); np.fill_diagonal(S, 0)
S[S < 0.05] = 0                                          # drop very weak edges
P = S / np.maximum(S.sum(1, keepdims=True), 1e-12)
d, n = 0.85, len(doc); r = np.ones(n) / n
for _ in range(100): r = (1 - d) / n + d * P.T @ r
print("LexRank centrality:")
for s, v in sorted(zip(doc, r), key=lambda x: -x[1]): print(f"  {v:.3f}  {s[:60]}")

print("lead-1 baseline:", doc[0])
print("top-2 by LexRank:", [doc[i][:45] for i in sorted(np.argsort(-r)[:2])], "(kept in document order)")

code.title: MMR selection, pruning and ROUGE
code.explain: Runs MMR on the Rowling sentences (λ = 0.5 picks S1 then S3; λ = 1 picks the redundant S1, S2), prunes an attribution clause, and computes ROUGE-2 = 12/29 ≈ 0.41 and ROUGE-1 = 22/32 ≈ 0.69 with clipped counts over three references.
mistakes: Dividing by system n-grams (that's precision, not ROUGE recall).
code.notes: Tokenisation choices (e.g. hyphenated words) change counts slightly.
code.code:
"""MMR selection to avoid redundancy, sentence pruning, and ROUGE-N."""
from collections import Counter

# MMR with given relevance and pairwise similarity scores
sents = {"S1": "Author J.K. Rowling won her legal battle to ban an unofficial encyclopedia.",
         "S2": "A US judge ruled in favour of Rowling against the encyclopedia's publication.",
         "S3": "The judge said the book copied large portions of her novels without commentary.",
         "S4": "The publisher said it was disappointed and considering an appeal."}
rel = {"S1": 0.90, "S2": 0.88, "S3": 0.70, "S4": 0.60}
sim = {frozenset(p): v for p, v in {("S1", "S2"): 0.85, ("S1", "S3"): 0.35, ("S1", "S4"): 0.30,
                                     ("S2", "S3"): 0.40, ("S2", "S4"): 0.35, ("S3", "S4"): 0.20}.items()}
def mmr(lam, k=2):
    chosen = []
    while len(chosen) < k:
        def score(s): return lam * rel[s] - (1 - lam) * max([sim[frozenset((s, t))] for t in chosen], default=0)
        best = max((s for s in rel if s not in chosen), key=score)
        print(f"   lambda={lam}: pick {best} (MMR {score(best):.3f})")
        chosen.append(best)
    return chosen
print("top-2 by relevance only:", sorted(rel, key=rel.get, reverse=True)[:2], "(redundant)")
print("MMR:", mmr(0.5))
print("MMR:", mmr(1.0))

# Sentence realisation: prune an attribution clause
s = "Rebels agreed to talks with government officials, international observers said Tuesday."
print("pruned:", s.split(", international observers said")[0] + ".")

# ROUGE-N recall over multiple references, with clipped counts
def ngrams(t, n): w = t.lower().replace(".", "").split(); return Counter(zip(*[w[i:] for i in range(n)]))
refs = ["Water spinach is a green leafy vegetable grown in the tropics.",
        "Water spinach is a semi-aquatic tropical plant grown as a vegetable.",
        "Water spinach is a commonly eaten leaf vegetable of Asia."]
sys_out = "Water spinach is a leaf vegetable commonly eaten in tropical areas of Asia."
def rouge_n(system, references, n=2):
    X = ngrams(system, n); match = total = 0
    for r in references:
        R = ngrams(r, n); m = sum(min(c, X[g]) for g, c in R.items())
        print(f"   ref has {sum(R.values())} {n}-grams, matches {m}")
        match += m; total += sum(R.values())
    return match, total
m, t = rouge_n(sys_out, refs, 2)
print(f"ROUGE-2 = {m}/{t} = {m/t:.2f}")
m1, t1 = rouge_n(sys_out, refs, 1)
print(f"ROUGE-1 = {m1}/{t1} = {m1/t1:.2f}")
